documentation.range: Boa imperator and its subspecies range from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Mexico through Central America to Northwest Ecuador. The species was introduced into St. Croix, Cozumel Island (México) and Florida (United States). The subspecies Boa imperator imperator is distributed across the whole range and can be found on the mainland as well as on some islands (e.g Cayos Cochinos, Honduras). Boa imperator sabogae is endemic to the Pearl Islands, Panama.
documentation.population: Population abundance of Boa imperator on the mainland remains unknown. Abundance is poorly documented in island populations but B. i. imperator was described as common in coastal mangrove islets of Belize (Boback 2006). The total population size of the best-studied population, on Cayos Cochinos Menor (Honduras), was estimated to be 632 individuals (reflecting a density of 1,000 boas/km² - Reed et al. 2007). This species' abundance was certainly higher prior to over-collection for the pet trade (Reed et al. 2007).
documentation.habitats: Boa imperator inhabits a wide range of habitats from desert lowlands, savanna and cultivated fields to wet and dry tropical forests and high elevation cloud forests (Greene 1983, Russo 2009). Boa imperator can be found in all forest strata (Boback et al. 2000). Island forms are more arboreal in general (Reed et al. 2007). Boa imperator are known to consume lizards, birds, non-volant mammals (e.g. Agouti) and volant mammals (bats; reviewed in Reed and Rodda 2009). In Central America, Boa imperator generally reach a length of three meters (reviewed in Reed and Rodda 2009) but adults are smaller on islands than in mainland adjacent areas (Barbour and Loveridge 1929; Boback 2005, 2006; Reed et al. 2007). Mexican B. imperator are also smaller than central American individuals with an average length between 1.0 meter and 1.75 meter. In all B. imperator subspecies, females are larger and heavier than males (Reed and Rodda 2009). Boa imperator are ovoviviparous and females produce an average of 17.8 neonates per litter (Fitch 1985).
documentation.threats:
One of the main threats that impacts Boa imperator is over-collection for pet trade or skins. The case of Cayos Cochinos Islands boas perfectly illustrates this problem: Cayos Cochinos boas were over-collected to the point the form (pink) was thought to be extinct in the wild (Russo 2009). In addition, deforestation may cause a loss of suitable habitat and cause fragmentation of populations. Moreover, B. imperator are eradicated by humans because of increasing overlap between the ranges of B. imperator and human use of territory (Russo 2009).

This species is considered to be an invasive taxon, see: http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?si=1439&fr=1&sts=&lang=EN.
documentation.measures: This species is listed on CITES Appendix II. It occurs in protected areas throughout its range. There are no further conservation recommendations at this time.
documentation.use_trade: Because of its beauty, docility and relative ease of care, Boa imperator are appropriate for the pet trade. In the U.S.A. more than 100,000 boas (Boa imperator and B. constrictor) were imported in the 1990s (Reed 2005). 5,000 boas were reported to be collected from Cayos Cochinos Islands (Honduras) for the pet trade in a decade (Reed et al. 2007). Additionally, B. imperator and B. constrictor skins are used for decorative and leather-trade items. Between 1998 and 2002, 8,192 skins were imported to the United States (Schlaepfer et al. 2005) and 2,035 skin products were exported from Mexico between 1980 and 2001 (Arroyo-Quiroz et al. 2007). Despite the fact that this species is listed under CITES Appendix II, local trade of B. imperator remains underestimated by international records (Reed and Rodda 2009). Boa imperator are also hunted for meat, to make medicines and sometimes used in religious services in the United-States (Reed and Rodda 2009).
documentation.rationale: Boa imperator extends across a large range including protected areas.  Although it is collected for the skin and pet trade, this is not a major range-wide threat. There is no evidence of population declines across the range, although some isolated subpopulations are small and have suffered declines historically.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: Hynková et al. (2009) suggested that Boa imperator is likely to warrant recognition as a full species. This arrangement was further supported by Reynolds et al. (2014) and is followed here. Two subspecies are recognized: B. i. imperator and B. i. sabogae (Reynolds and Henderson, in press).
